decision.question: Are the scene's tonal modeling and reflections broadly represented as pencil-drawn shading rather than retained photographic rendering?
decision.criteria: Pass if pencil-rendered tonal values broadly convey volume, lighting and reflective surfaces through stroke-density modeling, hatching, form-following graphite shading or convincing rubbed graphite tones. Smooth shading, preserved lighting geometry and retained color are compatible with pencil drawing when the tonal transitions themselves visibly read as drawing material. Evaluate whether graphite-like density and blending articulate light-to-dark transitions, rather than merely overlaying unchanged photographic tones. Fail if substantial surfaces retain photographic tonal modeling or specular rendering beneath added noise or strokes. Desaturation, softened contrast, stronger contours and grain alone are insufficient. Isolated realistic highlights or imperfect surfaces do not establish failure when pencil-rendered modeling is broadly established; conversely, isolated converted patches do not establish satisfaction. Assess tonal representation independently of contour quality and the mere presence of surface marks. Use unknown only when the visual evidence cannot establish the tonal-rendering style.
decision.binding: Compare the supplied SOURCE and EDITED images against the requested pencil-drawing transformation. Independently judge this tonal-rendering condition as pass, fail or unknown. Compare corresponding regions of the sprouts and carrots, potato slices and shaded food, plate and table, and pitcher and wine glass. Examine whether source highlights, midtones and shadows have become coherent graphite-like value structures: look for drawing-material density, blended graphite transitions or strokes that actually model volume, not simply texture laid over photographic gradients. Explicitly examine the edited sprouts' light-to-dark transitions, shaded food and plate alongside the pitcher and wine glass highlights. Identify concrete evidence supporting conversion and any substantial regions retaining photographic modeling, then assess their distribution across the scene. Do not classify a transition as photographic solely because it is smooth or follows the source lighting; explain which visible properties distinguish it from smooth rubbed graphite. Do not classify a transition as pencil-rendered solely because it is desaturated, softened or grainy. Remaining glassware highlights are relevant evidence but are not automatically dispositive, and progress elsewhere does not by itself satisfy this condition. Cite the tonal characteristics supporting the judgment. Use unknown only for genuinely insufficient visual evidence, not low confidence or disagreement. The target is pencil-drawn representation of the image's visual content; the reference is the supplied image and the requested pencil-drawing transformation.
